title: Chapter 74 — The Sperm Whale’s Head—Contrasted View
paragraphs: Here, now, are two great whales, laying their heads together. Let us join them and lay our own together.

Of the grand order of folio leviathans, the Sperm Whale and the Right Whale are by far the most remarkable. They are the only whales that man hunts regularly. To the Nantucketer they represent the two extremes among all the known kinds of whale. Since the outward difference between them shows mainly in their heads, and since a head of each is hanging from the Pequod's side at this very moment, and since we can move freely from one to the other simply by stepping across the deck — where, I'd like to know, could you find a better chance to study practical cetology than here?

In the first place, you are struck by the general contrast between these heads. Both are massive enough, heaven knows; but there is a certain mathematical symmetry in the Sperm Whale's that the Right Whale's sadly lacks. There is more character in the Sperm Whale's head. As you look at it, you find yourself involuntarily granting him an immense superiority in pervading dignity. In the present instance, too, this dignity is heightened by the pepper-and-salt color of his head at the summit, a sign of advanced age and long experience. In short, he is what the fishermen technically call a "gray-headed whale."

Let us now note what is least dissimilar in these heads — namely, the two most important organs: the eye and the ear. Far back on the side of the head, and low down, near the angle of either whale's jaw, if you search carefully, you will at last see a lashless eye, which you would think belonged to a young colt — it is so disproportionately small.

Now, from this peculiar sideways position of the whale's eyes, it is plain that he can never see an object that is exactly ahead, any more than one that is exactly astern. In a word, the position of the whale's eyes corresponds to that of a man's ears; and you may imagine for yourself how it would go with you if you surveyed objects sideways through your ears. You would find that you could command only some thirty degrees of vision forward of the straight side-line of sight, and about thirty more behind it. If your bitterest enemy were walking straight toward you in broad daylight with a dagger raised, you would not be able to see him, any more than if he were creeping up on you from behind. In a word, you would have two backs, so to speak; but at the same time also two fronts (side fronts): for what is it that makes the front of a man — what, indeed, but his eyes?

Moreover, in most other animals that I can now think of, the eyes are so placed as to blend their visual power imperceptibly, producing one picture for the brain and not two. But the peculiar position of the whale's eyes, effectively divided as they are by many cubic feet of solid head, which towers between them like a great mountain separating two lakes in valleys, must of course wholly separate the impressions that each independent organ conveys. The whale, therefore, must see one distinct picture on this side and another distinct picture on that side, while all between must be profound darkness and nothingness to him. Man, in effect, may be said to look out on the world from a sentry-box with two joined sashes for his window. But in the whale these two sashes are set in separately, making two distinct windows, but sadly impairing the view. This peculiarity of the whale's eyes is something always to be borne in mind in the fishery, and to be remembered by the reader in some later scenes.

A curious and most puzzling question might be raised about this matter of the Leviathan's vision. But I must be content with a hint. So long as a man's eyes are open in the light, the act of seeing is involuntary; that is, he cannot help mechanically seeing whatever objects are in front of him. Nevertheless, anyone's experience will teach him that, though he can take in an undiscriminating sweep of things at one glance, it is quite impossible for him to examine any two things attentively and completely — however large or however small — at one and the same instant of time, even if they lie side by side and touch each other. But if you now separate these two objects and surround each with a circle of profound darkness, then, in order to see one of them in such a way as to bring your mind to bear on it, you will utterly shut the other out of your consciousness at that moment. How is it, then, with the whale? True, both his eyes, in themselves, must act simultaneously; but is his brain so much more comprehensive, combining and subtle than man's that he can at the same moment attentively examine two distinct prospects, one on one side of him and the other in exactly the opposite direction? If he can, then it is as marvelous a thing in him as if a man were able to work through the proofs of two distinct problems in Euclid simultaneously. Nor, strictly investigated, is there anything incongruous in this comparison.

It may be only an idle whim, but it has always seemed to me that the extraordinary wavering movements some whales display when beset by three or four boats, and the timidity and liability to odd frights so common in such whales — that all this, I think, comes indirectly from the helpless perplexity of will in which their divided and diametrically opposite powers of vision must involve them.

But the whale's ear is every bit as curious as his eye. If you know nothing at all about the species, you could search these two heads for hours without ever finding that organ. The ear has no outer flap at all, and the hole itself is so wonderfully small that you could hardly push a quill into it. It sits a little behind the eye. Where their ears are concerned, there is one important difference to note between the sperm whale and the right whale: the sperm whale's ear opens to the outside, while the right whale's is completely and smoothly covered with a membrane, so that it cannot be seen from outside at all.

Is it not curious that so vast a being as the whale should see the world through so small an eye, and hear the thunder through an ear smaller than a hare's? But if his eyes were as broad as the lens of Herschel's great telescope, and his ears as capacious as the porches of cathedrals, would that make him any longer of sight, or any sharper of hearing? Not at all. Why, then, do you try to "enlarge" your mind? Make it subtler.

Let us now, with whatever levers and steam-engines we have at hand, tip the sperm whale's head over so that it lies bottom up; then, climbing a ladder to the summit, take a peep down the mouth; and if the body were not now completely separated from it, we might go down with a lantern into the great Kentucky Mammoth Cave of his stomach. But let us hold on here by this tooth and look about us where we are. What a really beautiful and chaste-looking mouth! From floor to ceiling it is lined, or rather papered, with a glistening white membrane, glossy as bridal satin.

But step outside now and look at this ominous lower jaw, which looks like the long narrow lid of an enormous snuffbox, hinged at one end instead of along one side. If you pry it up over your head so that its rows of teeth show, it looks like a fearsome portcullis — and that, sadly, is just what it proves to be for many a poor soul in the fishery, when these spikes come down on him with impaling force. But it is far more terrible to see when, fathoms down in the sea, you spot some sulky whale hanging there motionless, his huge jaw, some fifteen feet long, dangling straight down at right angles to his body, for all the world like a ship's jib-boom. This whale is not dead; he is just discouraged — out of sorts, perhaps; hypochondriac; and so limp that the hinges of his jaw have gone slack, leaving him in that awkward predicament, a disgrace to his whole tribe, who, no doubt, must be wishing lockjaw on him.

In most cases this lower jaw — being easily unhinged by a practiced hand — is detached and hoisted on deck for the purpose of extracting the ivory teeth and furnishing a supply of that hard white whalebone with which the fishermen fashion all sorts of curious articles, including canes, umbrella-sticks, and handles for riding-whips.

The jaw is hauled on board with a long, weary hoist, like an anchor; and when the right time comes — a few days after the other work — Queequeg, Daggoo, and Tashtego, all skilled dentists, are put to pulling teeth. Queequeg lances the gums with a sharp cutting-spade; then the jaw is lashed down to ringbolts, a tackle is rigged from aloft, and they drag out the teeth the way Michigan oxen drag old oak stumps out of wild woodland. Usually there are forty-two teeth in all; in old whales they are much worn down but not decayed, and not filled in our artificial way either. Afterward the jaw is sawn into slabs and stacked away like joists for building houses.
